what: Creativity as combination — how a piece stays a format that already works and still comes out new. Every idea is a new combination of things that already exist; the craft is choosing which proven core to keep and which one or two things to combine into it. The tells layer removes the average; this layer replaces it with something the viewer has not seen in quite this way before.
added: 2026-10-13 — the owner: 'it actually leverages creativity which is simply combining concepts and processing a slightly more unique outcome than the previous idea. that leads to formats that already work but they're innovative.'

source.rule: A row marked `research` names the work in `receipts` it rests on. Every other row is craft, marked `source: "craft"`.

master_rule: KEEP THE PROVEN CORE, COMBINE ONE OR TWO THINGS INTO IT. The work that lands hardest is mostly conventional with a small intrusion of the unusual — and people prefer what is novel and still recognisable. So the swipe's structure, its emotional map and its argument stay; the newness comes from one or two deliberate combinations the viewer can recognise both halves of.
one_line_test: Every combination can be said in one line: `<the proven thing>, but <the thing combined into it>`. A combination that needs a paragraph is two ideas or none.
remit_rule: The creative pass changes how a piece looks, sounds and what it leans on — the look, the setting's dressing, the reference world, the delivery style, a B-roll face, the opening picture, the sound. A move that would change the structure — the format, the order, the roles, the argument, the emotional map — is printed as a PROPOSAL for the owner and never applied; the structure lock decides it.

axes.name: The look
axes.what: The visual style the piece is made in.

axes.name: The setting
axes.what: Where it takes place, and how that place is dressed.

axes.name: The reference world
axes.what: The show, format, meme or world the piece leans on for timing and feel.

axes.name: The delivery
axes.what: How it is performed — the delivery style and register.

axes.name: Who carries a beat
axes.what: The person, character or object a B-roll beat is given to.

axes.name: The sound
axes.what: The bed, the drop-outs, the one sound that lands.

axes.name: The opening picture
axes.what: What is on screen in the first second.

axes.name: The format
axes.what: What kind of video it is.

axes.name: The emotional arc
axes.what: The shape of the feeling across the piece.

moves.name: One-axis swap
moves.what: Keep everything and change exactly one axis on purpose.
moves.how: Pick the axis the audience will notice first — usually the setting or the look — and move it somewhere they know but have never seen this format in.
moves.example: A routine filmed in a bathroom, moved to a car parked outside work at 7am.
moves.risk: A swap the audience does not recognise is just a strange choice.

moves.name: Category transplant
moves.what: A format proven in another category, carried onto our product.
moves.how: The chain already does this when the swipe comes from another category: the structure is theirs, the product is ours, and the friction between them is the newness.
moves.example: A cooking-video format used for a product that is not food — everything laid out, measured, combined.
moves.risk: Carried without translation, the format's own category leaks through and confuses what is being sold.

moves.name: Reference collision
moves.what: Two worlds the audience already knows, meeting where they never met.
moves.how: Take one reference from the culture read or culture map and play the piece in its frame — its narration, its camera, its music — while the content stays ours.
moves.example: A nature-documentary narration over someone choosing what to wear.
moves.risk: Works only when the room knows BOTH frames; a reference they don't share is noise.

moves.name: The literal metaphor
moves.what: Stage the room's own phrase literally on screen.
moves.how: Find a phrase the avatar actually uses about the problem in the language bank, and film it as if it were true.
moves.example: A room that says it is 'drowning in it' — shown as a person standing fully dressed in a slowly filling bath.
moves.risk: A phrase the writer invented is not the room's; it has to be quoted from the bank.

moves.name: Inversion
moves.what: Flip one expected role or order.
moves.how: The skeptic is the expert, the result comes first and the problem last, the product is the underdog — one flip, inside the swipe's roles.
moves.example: The before-and-after told backwards: the result first, then the morning it started.
moves.risk: An inversion of the structure is a proposal, not a creative-pass change.

moves.name: A new lens
moves.what: The same moment seen from somewhere unexpected.
moves.how: The mirror's view, the bystander's phone, the object on the shelf — the camera's position changes, the story does not.
moves.example: The routine filmed from inside the bathroom cabinet as it opens and closes.
moves.risk: A lens that hides the product or the face the beat depends on loses the beat.

moves.name: Honest exaggeration
moves.what: One true detail scaled up until it is funny or striking — the claim stays exactly true.
moves.how: Take a real, specific frustration and show it bigger than life; never exaggerate a result.
moves.example: The pile of products that did not work, stacked to the ceiling.
moves.risk: Exaggerating the product's result is a false claim; only the problem may be scaled.

moves.name: The problem given a face
moves.what: The problem cast as a character — always the villain or the fool, never the customer.
moves.how: Governed by the humor rules in the delivery slice.
moves.example: The problem as an uninvited houseguest who will not leave.
moves.risk: A problem character the customer could read as themself turns the joke on them.

rules.rule: Mostly conventional, a small intrusion of the unusual: one combination, two at most. Five new things at once is no format at all.

Most advanced, yet acceptable: the viewer must recognise both halves of a combination. Each half comes from the swipe, the culture read, the culture map or the bank, with its receipt; only the combination is ours.

Write three combinations, never one. The first is the average idea by construction. Pick the one that is furthest from what this brand has made and still instantly recognisable; print the other two as the alternates.
Put the combination where attention is decided — the opening picture, the setting, the look, the reference world. Never on the claim, the proof or the offer: those stay plain.
A move inside the creative pass's remit is applied. A move on the format, order, roles, argument or emotional map is printed as a proposal for the owner and never applied.
A combination is new against the brand's own work, not against the category: name what it differs from in what is already running, and leave the scoring to the creative-diversity check.
Newness comes from a specific real thing in an unexpected place — never from randomness. A combination that is only strange is the generator's average in a costume.

examples_note: Every example here is illustrative — the shape of a move, never content for a brief. What fills a move comes from the swipe, the room and the brand files.

receipts.cite: Young, J. W. (1940). A Technique for Producing Ideas. Advertising Publications.
receipts.what: An idea is nothing more nor less than a new combination of old elements — and the first ones produced are rarely the good ones.

receipts.cite: Koestler, A. (1964). The Act of Creation. Hutchinson.
receipts.what: Bisociation: creative leaps come from connecting two frames of reference that had never met.

receipts.cite: Uzzi, B., Mukherjee, S., Stringer, M. & Jones, B. (2013). Atypical combinations and scientific impact. Science, 342(6157), 468–472.
receipts.what: Across 17.9 million papers, the highest-impact work was grounded in conventional combinations with an intrusion of unusual ones — and twice as likely to be a hit.

receipts.cite: Hekkert, P., Snelders, D. & van Wieringen, P. C. W. (2003). 'Most advanced, yet acceptable': Typicality and novelty as joint predictors of aesthetic preference in industrial design. British Journal of Psychology, 94, 111–124.
receipts.what: People prefer designs that are both typical and novel at once — Loewy's MAYA principle, measured.
